lld-method:0.prompt: The interviewer says 'Design a parking lot.' What should you do first?
options: Start writing the ParkingLot class so there is code on the board early
Draw the full class diagram with every pattern you might use
Clarify requirements and scope: users, use cases, constraints and what's out of scope
Pick a database and design its tables
lld-method:0.explanation: LLD prompts are deliberately vague; clarifying scope (vehicle types, payments, multiple floors, concurrency) decides which entities matter. Jumping to code or patterns risks solving the wrong problem.

lld-method:0.prompt: During entity identification, what is the usual heuristic for reading the requirements?
options: Every sentence becomes one class
Nouns suggest candidate classes or attributes; verbs suggest methods and responsibilities
Adjectives become interfaces and adverbs become enums
Only words the interviewer repeats become classes
lld-method:0.explanation: Noun/verb analysis gives a first list ('a vehicle parks in a spot, gets a ticket'), which you then prune: some nouns are just attributes (color) and some are out of scope.

lld-method:0.prompt: A candidate spends 25 of 45 minutes writing polished code for a vending machine before asking any questions. What is the main risk?
options: The code may be too fast and confuse the interviewer
Interviewers never look at code in LLD rounds
The candidate will run out of whiteboard space
They may build the wrong thing and miss the requirements and trade-offs the interviewer wanted to discuss
lld-method:0.explanation: LLD rounds assess requirement gathering, modeling and reasoning as well as code. Late discoveries (e.g. 'it must support refunds') force rewrites and leave no time for extensibility or concurrency discussion.

lld-method:0.prompt: In an e-commerce design, an OrderLine only exists as part of one Order and is deleted with it. Which relationship models this best?
options: Composition
Aggregation
Plain association
Inheritance
lld-method:0.explanation: Composition means the part's lifecycle is owned by the whole. Aggregation is a weaker 'has-a' where parts can exist independently (a Team and its Players). OrderLine is not a kind of Order, so inheritance is wrong.

lld-method:0.prompt: Midway through, the interviewer asks: 'Later we'll add EV charging spots with per-kWh billing.' What is the strongest response?
options: Rewrite the allocation code now with an if-branch for EV spots everywhere
Show the extension point, e.g. a new spot type and a pricing strategy, so existing allocation code doesn't change
Say it's out of scope and continue with the original design
Add a boolean isEV to every class in the system
lld-method:0.explanation: Interviewers probe extensibility. Pointing to where a new SpotType and FeeStrategy plug in (Open/Closed) shows the design absorbs change. Scattered if-branches or flags show it doesn't.

lld-method:0.prompt: Car, Bike and Truck differ only in which spot sizes they can use. Which model is most appropriate?
options: A deep hierarchy Vehicle -> MotorVehicle -> FourWheeler -> Car, each overriding fits()
Separate unrelated classes for each vehicle with duplicated fields
A switch on the vehicle's class name inside every service
One Vehicle class with a size/type enum that the allocation logic uses
lld-method:0.explanation: When variants differ only by data, an attribute is simpler than subclasses; introduce subclasses only when behavior genuinely differs. Deep hierarchies and class-name switches are common LLD anti-patterns.

lld-method:0.prompt: Why define the public API (e.g. `parkVehicle(v): Ticket`, `exit(ticketId): Receipt`) before writing the classes' internals?
options: It pins down the contract clients rely on, which drives what classes and data you need
Interviewers grade only on method names
It lets you skip writing any implementation
TypeScript needs method signatures before class fields can be declared
lld-method:0.explanation: The API turns use cases into concrete operations and reveals which objects must collaborate. It's a design step, not a substitute for implementation.

lld-method:0.prompt: Which questions are worth clarifying at the start of an LLD round? Select all that apply.
options: Scale and concurrency, e.g. one machine or many entry gates at once
Which features are in scope (payments, reservations, notifications)
The interviewer's favourite editor
Pricing rules and edge cases such as lost tickets or overstays
Which logo the product will use
lld-method:0.explanation: Concurrency, scope and business rules change the model. Tooling preferences and branding don't affect the design.

lld-method:0.prompt: What do interviewers typically evaluate in an LLD round? Select all that apply.
options: Clear, cohesive responsibilities for each class
Extensibility for the likely changes they mention
Handling concurrency where it actually matters
Using as many named design patterns as possible
lld-method:0.explanation: Good LLD shows sound responsibilities, sensible extension points and awareness of races. Forcing patterns in without a reason is a red flag, not a plus.

lld-method:0.prompt: In an LLD interview, it's better to name a design pattern only when it solves a concrete problem in your design than to force patterns in.
options: True
False
lld-method:0.explanation: Saying 'pricing varies by vehicle and time, so I'll use a Strategy' shows judgement. Listing patterns without a need suggests memorization.

lld-method:0.prompt: You should design classes for every conceivable future requirement before writing any code.
options: True
False
lld-method:0.explanation: Over-engineering wastes interview time and adds complexity (YAGNI). Design for the stated requirements plus the likely changes the interviewer hints at.

lld-method:1.prompt: In a UML class diagram, a line from Order to OrderLine has a filled (black) diamond at the Order end. What does it mean?
options: Aggregation: OrderLines can exist without the Order
Composition: OrderLines are owned by the Order and die with it
Inheritance: OrderLine is a subclass of Order
Dependency: Order uses OrderLine temporarily as a parameter
lld-method:1.explanation: A filled diamond is composition, with the diamond on the whole's side. A hollow diamond is aggregation; a hollow triangle is generalization; a dashed arrow is dependency.

lld-method:1.prompt: In a UML class diagram, CardPayment has a dashed line with a hollow triangle pointing to «interface» PaymentMethod. What does this show?
options: CardPayment extends a PaymentMethod base class
CardPayment depends on PaymentMethod at runtime
CardPayment realizes (implements) the PaymentMethod interface
CardPayment is composed of PaymentMethod objects
lld-method:1.explanation: A dashed line with a hollow triangle is realization (implements). A solid line with a hollow triangle is generalization (extends). A plain dashed arrow is a dependency.

lld-method:1.prompt: In a UML class box, an attribute is written as `- balance: number`. What does the `-` mean?
options: Private visibility
Protected visibility
A static member
A derived (computed) attribute
lld-method:1.explanation: UML visibility markers: + public, - private, # protected, ~ package. Static members are underlined and derived attributes are prefixed with '/'.

lld-method:1.prompt: An association is drawn as Customer `1` ---- `0..*` Order. How should it be read?
options: Each customer has exactly one order, and each order has many customers
Each customer has zero or more orders, and each order belongs to exactly one customer
Customers and orders have a many-to-many relationship
An order may exist without any customer
lld-method:1.explanation: Each multiplicity sits next to the class it constrains: '0..*' next to Order means a customer has any number of orders; '1' next to Customer means each order has exactly one customer.

lld-method:1.prompt: In a UML sequence diagram, what does a solid line with a filled arrowhead from Gate to TicketService show?
options: A return message carrying a result back to the caller
An asynchronous message that doesn't wait for a reply
The creation of a new TicketService object
A synchronous call where Gate waits for TicketService to respond
lld-method:1.explanation: Solid line + filled arrowhead = synchronous message. Asynchronous messages use an open arrowhead; returns are dashed lines; creation is a dashed message to the new object's head, often labelled «create».

lld-method:1.prompt: You want a sequence diagram to show: 'if payment succeeds, issue a ticket; otherwise release the spot.' Which combined fragment fits?
options: opt
alt
loop
par
lld-method:1.explanation: alt shows mutually exclusive alternatives with guards ([success] / [else]). opt is a single optional block with one guard, loop repeats, and par shows parallel regions.

lld-method:1.prompt: A Department has Professors, but professors exist independently and can move between departments. Which UML relationship fits best?
options: Composition (filled diamond at Department)
Generalization (Professor extends Department)
Aggregation (hollow diamond at Department)
Realization (dashed line with hollow triangle)
lld-method:1.explanation: Aggregation is a whole-part 'has-a' where parts outlive the whole. Composition would mean deleting the department deletes its professors, which contradicts the requirement.

lld-method:1.prompt: TicketService.issue(clock: Clock) uses a Clock passed as a parameter but never stores it. How is this best shown in a class diagram?
options: A dependency: a dashed arrow from TicketService to Clock
A composition: a filled diamond at TicketService
An association with multiplicity 1 stored as a field
A generalization: TicketService extends Clock
lld-method:1.explanation: A dependency (dashed open arrow) means 'uses temporarily', e.g. as a parameter or local. An association implies a lasting structural link such as a field.

lld-method:1.prompt: What are sequence diagrams good for in an LLD discussion? Select all that apply.
options: Showing the order of calls between objects in one scenario
Showing which object owns each responsibility in a flow
Listing every attribute of every class
Distinguishing synchronous from asynchronous interactions
Showing inheritance hierarchies
lld-method:1.explanation: Sequence diagrams capture dynamic behavior over time for a use case. Attributes and inheritance are static structure, which belongs in class diagrams.

lld-method:1.prompt: Which UML class-diagram notations are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An italic class name or {abstract} marks an abstract class
The «interface» stereotype marks an interface
Static members are underlined
A dashed line with a filled diamond means composition
lld-method:1.explanation: Italics or {abstract}, «interface» and underlining for statics are standard. Composition uses a solid line with a filled diamond; there's no dashed-diamond notation.

lld-method:1.prompt: In UML, composition implies that when the whole is destroyed, its parts are destroyed too.
options: True
False
lld-method:1.explanation: Composition means exclusive ownership and a shared lifecycle; a part belongs to at most one whole at a time.

lld-method:1.prompt: In a UML sequence diagram, time flows from left to right across the lifelines.
options: True
False
lld-method:1.explanation: Lifelines are arranged left to right, and time flows from top to bottom. Messages lower on the diagram happen later.

lld-method:2.prompt: Which set of core entities best fits a multi-floor Parking Lot design?
options: ParkingLot, Level, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, Ticket, and a fee calculator
Driver, Car, Engine, Tyre and SteeringWheel
Server, Database, Cache and LoadBalancer
Ticket only, with every other concept stored as fields
lld-method:2.explanation: These map directly to the use cases: find a spot on a level, issue a ticket, compute the fee on exit. Car internals are out of scope, and infrastructure components belong in HLD.

lld-method:2.prompt: Parking fees vary: hourly on weekdays, a flat weekend rate, and an EV surcharge, with more rules likely. Which design fits best?
options: A long if/else in Ticket.computeFee()
A FeeStrategy interface with one implementation per rule, chosen when the vehicle exits
A subclass of ParkingLot for each pricing rule
Hard-coding the rates as constants in the exit gate
lld-method:2.explanation: Pricing is a family of interchangeable algorithms, so Strategy lets new rules be added without editing existing code. Subclassing the lot per rule mixes unrelated concerns.

lld-method:2.prompt: You must always assign the free spot nearest to the entrance for a given size. Which structure gives O(log n) allocation and release?
options: A hash set of free spot ids per size
An unsorted array of all spots scanned on every request
A min-heap of free spots per size, keyed by distance
A singly linked list of free spots in insertion order
lld-method:2.explanation: A min-heap pops the nearest free spot and re-inserts released ones in O(log n). A hash set is O(1) but can't give 'nearest'; an array scan is O(n); a linked list loses distance ordering.

lld-method:2.prompt: Gates run as several Node processes sharing a PostgreSQL database. Two cars at different gates get the same spot. What is the right fix?
options: Rely on Node being single-threaded to serialize allocations
Retry the allocation after a random delay whenever it looks busy
Cache free spots in each process's memory to reduce DB load
Allocate atomically in the DB, e.g. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or a conditional UPDATE that checks the spot is still free
lld-method:2.explanation: Separate processes don't share an event loop, so the DB must serialize: row locks or compare-and-set updates let only one transaction claim a spot. Per-process caches make the race worse.

lld-method:2.prompt: In a single Node process, two park() calls run concurrently. What is the bug?
options: findFree() throws because it isn't async
Another park() can run during the await and find the same free spot; occupy it before awaiting or reserve it atomically
issueTicket() runs before occupy() because of hoisting
There is no bug, since Node is single-threaded and code never interleaves
lld-method:2.explanation: Single-threaded doesn't mean atomic across an await: the check (findFree) and the act (occupy) are separated by a suspension point. Do the check-and-occupy synchronously, then await the side effects.

lld-method:2.prompt: Motorcycles fit any spot, cars fit compact or large, and trucks fit only large. Where should this rule live?
options: In one place, e.g. a compatibility map or spot.canFit(vehicle), used by the allocator
Duplicated in the entry gate, exit gate and display board
Inside each Ticket so it can be checked on exit
In the UI, which filters spots before calling the API
lld-method:2.explanation: Centralizing the fit rule means a new size or vehicle type changes one place. Duplicating it causes drift, and UI-only checks can be bypassed.
Partial hours round up, with a one-hour minimum: 30 min is 1 hour (10), 61 min is 2 hours (20), 120 min is 2 hours (40), and 0 min still bills the 1-hour minimum (20).

lld-method:2.prompt: Which edge cases should a strong Parking Lot answer mention? Select all that apply.
options: A lost ticket and how the fee is then charged
The lot being full when a car arrives
A payment failure at the exit gate
The brand of tyres on each vehicle
lld-method:2.explanation: Lost tickets, full capacity and failed payments are realistic flows interviewers probe. Tyre brand has no effect on parking logic.

lld-method:2.prompt: Which design choices for a Parking Lot follow SOLID principles? Select all that apply.
options: Pricing behind a FeeStrategy interface so new rules don't modify Ticket (OCP)
One ParkingLot class that handles allocation, payments, printing and DB access
The allocator depends on a SpotRepository interface rather than a concrete database client (DIP)
Spot subclasses whose park() throws for vehicle types the base class says are supported
Separate EntryGate and ExitGate classes, each with one job (SRP)
lld-method:2.explanation: Strategy for pricing, depending on abstractions and focused gate classes are SOLID. A do-everything ParkingLot breaks SRP, and subclasses that reject what the base type promises break LSP.

lld-method:2.prompt: Modeling each spot size as its own subclass is mandatory; a size enum on a single ParkingSpot class is considered wrong.
options: True
False
lld-method:2.explanation: If spot sizes differ only in data, an enum is simpler and perfectly acceptable. Subclasses make sense when spots differ in behavior (e.g. EV spots that track charging).

lld-method:2.prompt: Making ParkingLot a hard-wired Singleton makes unit tests harder unless the instance can be injected or reset.
options: True
False
lld-method:2.explanation: A global instance carries state between tests and can't easily be replaced with a fake. Creating one instance at the composition root and injecting it keeps 'one lot' without the testing pain.

lld-method:3.prompt: Which set of classes best captures the core of an Elevator System design?
options: Building, Wall, Window and Staircase
Elevator, Floor and a single global function that moves all cars
Elevator (car), Controller/Dispatcher, Request (hall and car calls), Door, and Direction/State
Passenger, Ticket, Payment and Receipt
lld-method:3.explanation: Cars with state, a dispatcher assigning requests, request types, doors and direction cover the behavior interviewers expect. Building structure and payments are out of scope.

lld-method:3.prompt: Which behavior describes the LOOK scheduling algorithm for one elevator?
options: Serve requests strictly in the order they arrived
Keep moving in the current direction, serving requests on the way, and reverse once none remain ahead
Always go to the closest requested floor, whichever direction it is
Travel to the top floor and bottom floor on every cycle
lld-method:3.explanation: LOOK sweeps in one direction and turns around at the last pending request. FCFS serves in arrival order, nearest-first can starve far floors, and always touching both ends is SCAN.

lld-method:3.prompt: What is the main problem with first-come-first-served scheduling for an elevator?
options: It can't handle more than one request at a time
It requires knowing every request in advance
It always starves the top floor
It causes lots of back-and-forth travel and passes floors with waiting requests without stopping
lld-method:3.explanation: Serving 9, then 2, then 8 makes the car zig-zag and ignore requests it passes, increasing wait and travel time. Direction-aware algorithms like LOOK fix that.

lld-method:3.prompt: Why should a design model hall calls and car calls as different kinds of request?
options: A hall call (floor + direction) can be served by any car and needs dispatching; a car call (destination) belongs to one car
Hall calls are always higher priority than car calls
Car calls must be stored in the database, while hall calls stay in memory
There's no real difference; it only affects the button colors
lld-method:3.explanation: Hall calls go to the dispatcher, which picks the best car; car calls are pressed inside a car and only that car can serve them. Mixing them makes dispatch logic tangled.

lld-method:3.prompt: Car A is at floor 3 moving up; car B is idle at floor 8. A hall call comes from floor 5, going up. Using a simple cost of distance plus a penalty for moving away, which car should be assigned?
options: Car B, because idle cars should always be preferred
Car B, because it is on a higher floor
Car A, because floor 5 is on its way in the same direction and only 2 floors away
Neither; the request must wait until a car is idle at floor 5
lld-method:3.explanation: A is heading up and will pass floor 5 after 2 floors with no penalty, while B is 3 floors away. Preferring cars already moving toward the call in the same direction is the core dispatch heuristic.

lld-method:3.prompt: A car's state is DoorsOpen and a new car call arrives for floor 7. What should the state machine do?
options: Start moving immediately with the doors open
Ignore the call because the car is busy
Throw an error and reset the car to Idle
Queue the call; the car may move only after the doors close
lld-method:3.explanation: Safety rules belong in the state machine: from DoorsOpen the only move transition goes through DoorsClosed. Requests are recorded and served afterwards, never dropped.
Moving up from 5, the car serves floors above in ascending order (6, 7, 9), then reverses and serves floors below in descending order (2, 1).

lld-method:3.prompt: Buttons on many floors send requests at any moment while each car's control loop is running. Which design avoids race conditions on a car's request list?
options: Let every button handler modify the car's request array directly
Send requests as events into a queue that a single controller loop per car processes, or synchronize access
Copy the request list into each button object
Poll every button once a minute and rebuild the list from scratch
lld-method:3.explanation: Funnelling inputs through a queue to one owner (actor-style) or locking access means only one writer at a time. Direct concurrent mutation from many sources is the classic race; minute-long polling hurts responsiveness.

lld-method:3.prompt: Which requirements are worth clarifying before designing an elevator system? Select all that apply.
options: Number of elevators and floors
Capacity or weight limits per car
Emergency and maintenance modes
The colour of the buttons
The dispatch goal, e.g. shortest wait vs lowest energy use
lld-method:3.explanation: Scale, capacity, special modes and the optimization goal all change the design. Button colour doesn't.

lld-method:3.prompt: Which design patterns fit naturally into an elevator system? Select all that apply.
options: State for car states (idle, moving up, moving down, doors open, maintenance)
Strategy for pluggable dispatch algorithms (nearest car, zoning, LOOK)
Observer to update floor displays when a car's position changes
Decorator to make each floor a Singleton
lld-method:3.explanation: Car behavior depends on state, dispatch policies are interchangeable, and displays react to position changes. 'Decorator to make floors singletons' mixes up two unrelated patterns and solves no problem here.

lld-method:3.prompt: In an elevator design, a hall call must be bound to one specific car the moment the button is pressed and can never be reassigned.
options: True
False
lld-method:3.explanation: Many dispatchers re-evaluate assignments as conditions change (a car fills up or goes into maintenance). Allowing reassignment improves wait times and handles failures.

lld-method:3.prompt: LOOK differs from SCAN in that the car reverses at the last pending request instead of travelling all the way to the end floor.
options: True
False
lld-method:3.explanation: SCAN sweeps to the physical end before reversing; LOOK only goes as far as the furthest request in that direction, saving travel.
